commit.message: implement issue #2297 : Add ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute to generated code

requirement.title: Add ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute to generated code.
requirement.summary: MessagePack-generated code should be decorated with ExcludeFromCodeCoverage so it does not skew coverage results. The thread includes a coverage-tool workaround and a proposed template-based implementation, but no maintainer decision on those proposals.

criteria.text: All MessagePack-generated code is decorated with ExcludeFromCodeCoverage.
criteria.summary: All MessagePack-generated code must use ExcludeFromCodeCoverage

criteria.text: Users can obtain the ExcludeFromCodeCoverage decoration without being required to configure a new setting; an optional setting is permissible but not required.
criteria.summary: ExcludeFromCodeCoverage must apply by default without requiring configuration

open_questions: Should the implementation follow armadavalor's proposal to add the fully qualified attribute to the formatter, string-key formatter, enum/union formatter, and resolver templates and update the verified snapshots, or should users instead be directed to coverage-tool configuration such as b-kurczynski-dl's dotnet-coverage exclusion?
Should generated types also receive GeneratedCode("MessagePack.SourceGenerator", <version>), as armadavalor suggested?
Should the attribute always be emitted, or should an optional setting control it?
requirement.short: MessagePack-generated code must have ExcludeFromCodeCoverage to avoid skewing coverage

lines: Learn more about using a mix of your own custom formatters and automatically generated ones in [the Analyzer section](#analyzer).
+All generated formatters and resolvers are decorated with `[ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]`, so generated code does not skew code coverage reports.
+The attribute is only emitted for targets where it is available (not `netstandard2.0` or .NET Framework).

[MagicOnion](https://github.com/Cysharp/MagicOnion) is a code-first gRPC framework based on grpc-dotnet and MessagePack. gRPC usually communicates with Protocol Buffers using IDL. But MagicOnion uses MessagePack for C# and does not need IDL. When communicating C# to C#, schemaless (or rather C# classes as schema) is better than using IDL.

suspicions.hypothesis: The new tests verify only that each generated file contains at least one attribute, not that every emitted type is decorated. A resolver file could retain its resolver-level attribute while FormatterCache<T> or GetFormatterHelper loses its attribute and both new tests would still pass.

Malformed or uncompilable generated code could pass the new tests because they inspect text only, ignore generator diagnostics, and never compile the output with NETSTANDARD2_0 or NETFRAMEWORK defined. Compiling the same source under both active and inactive guard configurations would probe this.

The premise that ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute is unavailable on .NET Framework may be too broad for the framework versions MessagePack supports. If a supported .NET Framework target already supplies the attribute, the NETFRAMEWORK guard unnecessarily leaves that output uncovered and makes the README/test explanation inaccurate.

The new test source may not exercise EnumTemplate despite its comment: MyEnum is not referenced by a generated object and the assertions do not require an enum-formatter file. If no standalone enum formatter is generated, removing the enum template's attribute could leave both coverage tests green.

The newly skipped EnumFormatter_CollidingTypeNames test could be exposing a regression caused by the edited enum output or whitespace generation rather than unrelated CI flakiness. Running that test repeatedly against the pre-change and post-change generator would distinguish the two.

probes.title: Composite resolver FormatterCache still decorated
probes.hypothesis: The change's per-type attribute placement leaves some generated type (e.g. FormatterCache<T> in the composite resolver, or the enum formatter when no standalone enum file is generated) undecorated, so the claim that all generated types carry the attribute on supported targets is false; the change's own tests only check each file has at least one attribute.
criteria: For each generated file, every top-level and nested type declaration line is immediately preceded (ignoring guard lines) by [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage].
probes.means: If this fails, at least one generated type (resolver-level, FormatterCache<T>, GetFormatterHelper, or a formatter) lacks the attribute even though every file contains one somewhere, disproving the 'all generated code is decorated' claim and exposing the weakness the writer suspected in the change's own tests.

rounds.reason: The assertion is related to the hypothesis, but both head and base fail with only a summary. The output does not include the assertion's list of allegedly undecorated types or any generated source, and it does not rule out an exception or a false positive from the probe's line-based declaration/attribute detection. Therefore it does not establish that the head failure was caused by the hypothesized missing decoration.

The output contains only a test-failure summary, with no assertion message, generated-type count, exception, or list of undecorated types. Consequently, it does not show whether the decoration assertion failed because changed code left types undecorated, whether the setup generated no types and tripped the guard assertion, or whether the probe threw another error. The equally terse base failure does not resolve that ambiguity.

The probe's hypothesis was that the change leaves some generated type (FormatterCache<T>, GetFormatterHelper, or an enum formatter) undecorated. Re-reading hunks H2-H11, every template that emits a type inside EmitNestingTypesAndNamespaces — the enum, object, string-key formatter, union formatter, resolver class, FormatterCache<T> in both resolvers, and GetFormatterHelper — receives the guarded attribute at the exact line preceding the type declaration. The composite resolver's FormatterCache<T> (H3) and the standard resolver's FormatterCache<T> (H7) and GetFormatterHelper (H8) are all decorated, and the enum template (H4) decorates its own formatter independent of whether a standalone enum file is generated. The only remaining candidate is a type the compiled probe would need to actually emit; but the probe's ambiguity (the failure summary with no assertion text) came from the probe constructing a driver via `CSharpGeneratorDriver.Create(new MessagePackGenerator())` and relying on ReferencesHelper/ReferencesSet members that may resolve differently or throw during setup rather than from a genuine undecorated type. Since the change's templates place the attribute on every emitted type inside the nesting scope, the hypothesis that a generated type loses its attribute does not hold at this branch head; there is nothing to anchor a corrected probe to. I give up rather than rewrite a probe for a hypothesis contradicted by the change itself.

probes.title: ExcludeFromCodeCoverage availability on .NET Framework
probes.hypothesis: ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute exists on supported .NET Framework targets (net472 etc.), so the `!NETFRAMEWORK` guard unnecessarily suppresses the attribute on .NET Framework, contradicting the README's claim that it is 'not available' on .NET Framework and leaving that output uncovered.
criteria: A net472 project referencing the real framework assemblies builds when the attribute is applied, proving the attribute is available on .NET Framework (so the NETFRAMEWORK guard is over-broad).
probes.means: If it builds, ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute is available on .NET Framework, so the `!NETFRAMEWORK` guard (and the README statement it justifies) is wrong: .NET Framework generated code is needlessly left undecorated.
probes.verdict: The probe project built, as the hypothesis predicts.

refusals.question: Is the template-based, automatically enabled design with no decoration at all for NETSTANDARD2_0 or NETFRAMEWORK the intended resolution of #2297, or does 'all MessagePack-generated code' require those targets to receive an attribute or compatibility declaration too?
refusals.why: The requirement says all generated code, while the implementation makes an availability-based exception, and the issue discussion records no maintainer decision between the proposed approaches. This is a requirement and behavior decision for the owner.
refusals.summary: Decide whether NETSTANDARD2_0 and NETFRAMEWORK exclusions satisfy #2297

refusals.question: Should EnumFormatter_CollidingTypeNames be disabled as part of this coverage-attribute change, or should its flakiness be reproduced, fixed, and tracked separately with the test left enabled here?
refusals.why: Skipping a test is unrelated scope and removes regression coverage for one of the edited formatter paths; the diff does not establish that the flakiness is pre-existing or who owns restoring the test.
refusals.summary: Decide whether EnumFormatter_CollidingTypeNames skip belongs here or separately tracked

refusals.question: Is the constrained-nesting newline change required to make the new preprocessor directives valid, and should its generated-output churn remain in #2297 rather than be split into a separate formatting fix?
refusals.why: This changes generation for constrained nesting types beyond simply adding an attribute. Its necessity and the branch/scope for a separate formatting correction are owner decisions.
refusals.summary: Confirm constrained-nesting newline necessity and scope for generated-output churn
